args.topic: Tenant's notice of the landlord's noncompliance

content:
The statute gives no set number of days for restoring hot water. Its only clock starts when you deliver a written notice, and the program's deadlines show none running, because you confirmed you have not delivered one.

Hot water is a duty the statute names for a unit that is not a single-family home or duplex, "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (Fla. Stat. 83.51(2)(a)). You confirmed yours is not a house or duplex. The tool found nothing on hot water or a water heater in your lease's text. Your lease does put plumbing and air-conditioning repair on the landlord (Lease Section 7.1).

Pay less rent: open, as a defense if the landlord sues for possession (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). It needs a written notice delivered to the landlord that names the problem and says you intend not to pay rent because of it, then 7 days. That notice is still to do. If the defense is made out, the court decides how much the rent is reduced (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). If the landlord files a case, you must pay the rent into the court registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after service to keep any defense other than payment (Fla. Stat. 83.60(2)). The tool does not compute that date.

End the lease: not settled (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)). It needs a written notice that names the problem and says you intend to end the lease, then 7 days without a fix. You confirmed you paid rent after you knew of the problem. The statute does not settle whether that waived ending the lease over a problem that is still not fixed (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)).
- Reading one: an unfixed problem is a continuing noncompliance, so paying does not waive it, and this option is open.
- Reading two: the noncompliance is the failure to fix a problem you already knew of, so paying waives it, and only a new or different failure starts over. Then this option is closed.

Two more points the statute does not settle reach both options.
- Which list the heater falls under. Fla. Stat. 83.56(1) and 83.60(1)(b) speak only of 83.51(1), which covers codes, structure, and plumbing, while hot water is named in 83.51(2)(a). On one reading, it is an 83.51(1) duty when a building, housing, or health code covers it (Fla. Stat. 83.51(3)). The tool does not hold those codes; your city or county code enforcement office can tell you. On the other, it is an 83.51(2) duty because that subsection names it, so neither notice route reaches it, and part II does not let you raise an 83.51(2) noncompliance as a defense to an action for possession (Fla. Stat. 83.51(2)(c)). On that reading the rent defense would not be open.
- What "material" means. Both 7-day periods need a landlord who "materially fails to comply" or a "material noncompliance" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1), 83.60(1)(b)). The statute does not define it. On one reading, failing a duty 83.51(1) lists is material whatever its size. On the other, it turns on how serious the condition is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living in the unit.

Your AC is separate. Your lease promises the landlord keeps the air-conditioning in good working order (Lease Section 7.1), and Fla. Stat. 83.56(1) also reaches "material provisions of the rental agreement", so that clause can support ending the lease over the AC. Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b) speaks only of 83.51(1), so a lease provision alone does not reach the rent defense.

Money back: the aggrieved party "may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance" (Fla. Stat. 83.55). The statute gives no formula and the tool computes no amount. Your lease says no interruption of services "entitles Resident to any reduction or abatement of Rent" when it is "caused by a provider, a repair, or anything beyond Landlord's reasonable control" (Lease Section 5.2). A lease term is "void and unenforceable" to the extent it waives the rights or remedies in this part or limits the landlord's liability under law (Fla. Stat. 83.47(1)). So Section 5.2 cannot take away what 83.60(1)(b) and 83.55 give. Whether it reaches a broken heater the landlord has not replaced is a point you can check against its words.

Cases, as the program printed them above:
- K.D. Lewis Enterprises Corp. v. Smith, 445 So. 2d 1032 (Fla. 5th DCA 1984), read the 1981 statute. Tenants withheld rent over upkeep and sued for the lost value of their apartments; you paid rent and have sued no one. The court said "it is necessary for the tenant to comply with section 83.56" to recover for the lost value (at 1037). You have not delivered a written notice, so a claim for lost value would need one first. It cuts against you today. The tenants there also lost possession when they did not pay the registry (at 1033), which is the 83.60(2) risk above.
- Lakeway Management Co. of Florida v. Stolowilsky, 527 So. 2d 950 (Fla. 3d DCA 1988), read the 1985 statute. Tenants stopped paying rent, and their first written complaint came only after the landlord's three-day notice; you have no such notice. The court called a written complaint the "condition precedent to urging constructive eviction" (at 951). You have not made one, so that defense would not be ready. It cuts against you today.
- Bennett M. Lifter, Inc. v. Varnado, 480 So. 2d 1336 (Fla. 3d DCA 1985), read the 1983 statute. A hot water heater was out for days and a child was burned; you report no injury. The court said the statute "requires a landlord to provide hot running water" (at 1341). That supports hot water as a landlord duty here. It says nothing on how long or on rent.
- Mansur v. Eubanks, 401 So. 2d 1328 (Fla. 1981), read the 1977 statute. A gas explosion followed an effort to get a gas water heater and stove working; no injury is in your facts. The court said the landlord must repair "dangerous defective conditions upon notice of their existence by the tenant" (at 1330). Your landlord has notice, but no danger is in your facts. K.D. Lewis says Mansur "did not create a new cause of action in tort for the diminution in value of the premises" (at 1038), so it does not help a claim for rent money.
- Solomon v. Gentry, 388 So. 2d 52 (Fla. 4th DCA 1980), read the 1979 statute. A bad heating unit led to a fire. The court held "no such warranty arises under a lease of real property" (at 53). It cuts against you: a claim has to rest on the statute and the lease, not an implied warranty.
- Ray v. Tampa Windridge Associates, 596 So. 2d 676 (Fla. 2d DCA 1991), read the 1985 statute. A tenant signed a release about locks. The court went on "even assuming" an agreement could relieve the 83.51(2)(a) duty, and found the release did not (at 677). It matters to you only if your lease relieves the hot water duty; the tool found nothing like that.
- Menendez v. Palms West Condo. Ass'n, 736 So. 2d 58 (Fla. 1st DCA 1999). A doorscope claim failed because neither the statute nor the lease required one (at 62). It differs from yours: the statute names hot water.
- Bennett v. Mattison, 382 So. 2d 873 (Fla. 1st DCA 1980), Paterson v. Deeb, 472 So. 2d 1210 (Fla. 1st DCA 1985), Haynes v. Lloyd, 533 So. 2d 944 (Fla. 5th DCA 1988), and Smith v. Grove Apartments, LLC, 976 So. 2d 582 (Fla. 3d DCA 2007) are injury suits over a hallway fall, locks and an attack, broken glass, and a parking lot. Bennett said a violation "would be evidence of negligence" (at 875), and Paterson said a violation "is at least evidence of negligence" (at 1216). You report no injury, so they do not reach your rent question. Haynes called the common-area duty "not particularly relevant" there (at 945), and Smith applied it to a parking lot (at 586). Neither is about hot water.

args.topic: Tenant's notice of the landlord's noncompliance

content:
Sorry for the length. Short answer: it may count, but only if two things are true, and the tool cannot tell yet.

The statute asks for "written notice", not a letter, so typing it in the portal is writing (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)). The two points are:

- What it said. The notice that starts the 7 days must name the problem and say you intend to end the lease (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)) or not to pay rent (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). A request that only asks for a repair is written, but it is not that notice, and no 7 days run from it. The sheet will ask what each request said.
- How it was delivered. The statute lists mailing, delivering a true copy, e-mailing under 83.505, or leaving a copy if you are absent (Fla. Stat. 83.56(4)). Your lease says notices to the landlord go by hand to the leasing office, by certified mail, or by e-mail to the office address (Lease Section 13.1). The portal is the lease's channel for repair requests (Lease Section 7.1). Neither list names a portal message, and the text I have does not say whether one counts as delivery. E-mail delivery has its own conditions (Fla. Stat. 83.505(1)).

So if a request named an intention and a portal message counts as delivery, the 7 days run from its delivery. If either fails, no 7 days have started, and a new notice sent by a listed method would start them. The same two points apply to your AC request. The program's deadlines are waiting for you to confirm on the sheet that you delivered a written notice.

Cases, as already printed above:
- Lakeway Management Co. of Florida v. Stolowilsky, 527 So. 2d 950 (Fla. 3d DCA 1988), read the 1985 statute. Tenants who stopped paying rent made their first written complaint only after the landlord's three-day notice. The court called that complaint the "condition precedent to urging constructive eviction" (at 951). It shows a written complaint matters, but it does not say what form counts. You paid rent and have no three-day notice.
- K.D. Lewis Enterprises Corp. v. Smith, 445 So. 2d 1032 (Fla. 5th DCA 1984), read the 1981 statute. Tenants withheld rent over upkeep. The court said "it is necessary for the tenant to comply with section 83.56" to recover for the lost value of the premises (at 1037). It does not say whether a portal message is delivery. It cuts against you if your requests did not state an intention.

args.topic: Tenant's notice of the landlord's noncompliance

content:
You confirmed your portal request did not say you would end the lease or stop paying rent. So it is a written request, but not the notice in Fla. Stat. 83.56(1) or 83.60(1)(b), and the program's deadlines show no 7 days running from it.

Your options:
- Not paying rent over the problem: open (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). It needs a notice that names the problem and says you intend not to pay rent because of it, then 7 days. You said you do not want this one.
- Ending the lease: not settled (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)). It needs a notice that says you intend to end the lease, then 7 days without a fix. You paid rent after you knew of the problem, and the statute does not settle whether that waived ending the lease over a problem still unfixed (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)). If it did not, this option is open; if it did, it is closed.
- Asking for the repair and the rec center costs without stating either intention: a letter can ask for both, but it would start neither 7-day period, because those need one of the two intentions. The statute lets you recover "the damages caused by the noncompliance" (Fla. Stat. 83.55). K.D. Lewis Enterprises Corp. v. Smith, 445 So. 2d 1032, 1037 (Fla. 5th DCA 1984), tied a claim for the lost value of the premises to complying with 83.56, and it read the 1981 statute. Whether that reaches your rec center costs, the stored text and cases do not say.

Before I draft the letter I need three answers:
1. How many days to give the landlord to reply.
2. How you will send it. Your lease says a notice must be "in writing and delivered by hand to the leasing office", "sent by certified mail to that address", or "sent by e-mail to office@magnoliarow.example" (Lease Section 13.1).
3. Which posture:
- preserve: "Describes the condition and asks for the repair. Cites nothing."
- assert: "Adds the 83.51(1) duty, quoted."
- escalate: "Adds the 83.56(1) sentence, quoted."

Assert would quote the sentence in Fla. Stat. 83.51(1) that begins "The landlord at all times during the tenancy shall". Escalate would quote the sentence in Fla. Stat. 83.56(1) that begins "If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1)". A letter is the 83.56(1) or 83.60(1)(b) notice only if it states one of those two intentions.

args.topic: Tenant's notice of the landlord's noncompliance

content:
The choice is yours; I cannot pick it for you. What makes a letter count is not the posture. It is whether the letter states an intention.

The three postures, in the tool's own words:
- preserve: "Describes the condition and asks for the repair. Cites nothing."
- assert: "Adds the 83.51(1) duty, quoted."
- escalate: "Adds the 83.56(1) sentence, quoted."

The tool's note on all three says the letter "states your request and any sentences quoted above" and is the statute's notice "only if it states one of those intentions". The two intentions are to end the lease (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)) and not to pay rent (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). So on any posture:
- A letter that states neither is a written request on the record, and the statute's 7 days do not start from it.
- A letter that states one of them is the statute's notice, and its 7 days run from delivery.
- Assert and escalate add a quoted sentence of law. They do not add an intention. The escalate sentence is about ending the lease.

You said you do not want to threaten the landlord. That is a choice between a letter that asks and a letter that states an intention. The 7 days you give the landlord to reply are yours to set and are separate from the statute's 7 days.

Cases, as already printed above. Lakeway Management Co. of Florida v. Stolowilsky, 527 So. 2d 950, 951 (Fla. 3d DCA 1988), read the 1985 statute and called a written complaint the "condition precedent to urging constructive eviction", but it does not say what the complaint must state. K.D. Lewis Enterprises Corp. v. Smith, 445 So. 2d 1032, 1037 (Fla. 5th DCA 1984), read the 1981 statute and said "it is necessary for the tenant to comply with section 83.56" to recover for the lost value of the premises. So a later claim for lost value may need a notice that states the intention to end the lease. Whether rec center costs count as lost value, the cases do not say.

E-mail: your lease lists e-mail to office@magnoliarow.example (Lease Section 13.1). The statute's list says e-mailing "in accordance with s. 83.505" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(4)), and that section requires an addendum both sides signed agreeing to e-mail notices (Fla. Stat. 83.505(1)). Whether you signed one is for you to check. Your lease also lists hand delivery to the leasing office and certified mail.

Tell me which posture you choose. If you want the letter to state one of the two intentions, tell me which.
